title: Nearly two decades after the global financial crisis, a new regulatory era is dawning
gist: Basel III has entered a deregulatory 'modernization' phase led by the United States, with a re-proposed Basel III endgame estimated to cut capital requirements for the largest US banks by $60 billion, and the Bank of England and European Commission following with their own competitiveness-driven adjustments. The open questions are how far each jurisdiction goes, whether easing is procyclical, and whether internationally common standards fragment as countries adopt a wait-and-see stance.

insights.claim: The post-global-financial-crisis regulatory framework is entering a period of significant change, with the debate shifting from financial stability alone to whether rules have been correctly calibrated for domestic growth and competitiveness.
insights.so_what: A multi-year easing cycle in bank capital and liquidity rules is the base case — structurally supportive for bank ROE and capital return across the US, UK, and EU.
insights.quote: the internationally aligned regulatory framework built over the past fifteen years is entering a period of significant change
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: The United States is at the forefront of the deregulatory push, and no other member of the Basel Committee or Financial Stability Board has yet approached the scale of the work progressing in the US.
insights.so_what: The relative capital-relief gap favors US bank competitiveness versus UK and EU peers until other jurisdictions catch up.
insights.quote: No other member of the Basel Committee or FSB has yet approached the scale of the work progressing in the US.
insights.locator: First, how far will reform go across jurisdictions?
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reemphasized in summer 2025 the need for a fundamental revaluation of financial regulation, after which US banking agencies pursued a review of the prudential capital regime and re-proposed the Basel III endgame.
insights.so_what: Names the political origin and timeline of the US easing cycle — a top-down mandate, not an agency-level drift, so it is unlikely to reverse quickly.
insights.locator: In summer 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: The re-proposed Basel III endgame aims in part to simplify the regime by introducing a single set of risk-based capital calculations, addressing long-standing US criticism of gold-plating.
insights.so_what: A single capital stack removes the dual-stack binding constraint that has distorted US bank balance sheet allocation — watch which business lines get re-risked first.
insights.locator: Long considered controversial and criticized in the US
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Liquidity rules are the next front: analysts are questioning whether Basel III's short- and longer-term liquidity metrics have pushed banks to hold buffers that are excessive or misaligned with systemic resilience, reviving questions from COVID-19-era stress.
insights.so_what: Liquidity buffer relief would free HQLA-locked balance sheet and change bank demand for Treasuries and reserves — a plumbing effect with rates-market consequences.
insights.locator: Liquidity requirements have also come under renewed scrutiny.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: The shift extends beyond capital and liquidity to the transparency of bank stress tests and to notable changes in supervision and enforcement standards.
insights.so_what: Supervisory and enforcement loosening is harder to quantify than a capital ratio but drives realized credit risk appetite — the underappreciated part of the easing.
insights.locator: However, the debate extends beyond capital and liquidity.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman argues that robust bank capital levels can be maintained while removing regulatory barriers that harm credit availability without delivering commensurate stability benefits.
insights.so_what: The sitting supervision chair's framework — material risks, tailored to risk profile — is the template for what actually gets eased.
insights.locator: Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Current US proposals are estimated to reduce capital requirements for the largest US banks by $60 billion, which Fed Governor Michael Barr argues could create a sizeable hole in the safety net needed to stabilize the system in future stress.
insights.so_what: A $60 billion capital release is the hard number to size the buyback and balance-sheet-growth capacity unlocked at US G-SIBs — and the tail risk if it proves procyclical.
insights.locator: With the current proposals estimated to reduce capital requirements
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: A sitting Fed governor publicly asserts that the past year of US regulatory work has shifted the balance too far toward deregulation and threatens the safety and soundness of financial intermediation.
insights.so_what: An on-the-record dissent from inside the Fed Board is the seed of future reversal risk if a credit event occurs — headline risk for bank capital-return plans.
insights.quote: US regulatory efforts over the past year have shifted the balance too far toward deregulation
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

themes.theme: UK and EU follow on competitiveness grounds

insights.claim: The Bank of England announced in July that it would make targeted capital adjustments to rebalance requirements for domestic banks relative to their foreign competitors.
insights.so_what: Explicit level-playing-field motivation means UK bank capital relief is now tied to whatever the US does — a read-across trade between US and UK bank capital ratios.
insights.locator: The Bank of England (BofE), for example, announced in July
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: The European Commission published a banking-sector competitiveness strategy that sets the stage for EU legislative deliberations in 2027 on aspects of the Basel prudential rulebook, following calls from the European Banking Authority and European Central Bank to simplify parts of the single-market regime.
insights.so_what: 2027 is the concrete EU catalyst date — EU bank capital relief is a later-cycle story than the US or UK.
insights.locator: and the European Commission published a wider strategy
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Bank of England Governor and FSB Chair Andrew Bailey holds that deregulation for its own sake is undesirable and that effective, proportionate regulation can itself promote competitiveness, framing the debate as not a binary choice between regulation and growth.
insights.so_what: The FSB chair's framing caps how far UK easing goes and signals the international body will push back on the most aggressive proposals.
insights.locator: A similar view has been expressed by BofE Governor
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: EU officials have struck a more cautious tone, maintaining that it is essential not to jeopardize progress in correcting the deficiencies that caused the global financial crisis.
insights.so_what: Expect the widest transatlantic divergence in effective bank capital requirements since Basel III was agreed.
insights.locator: EU officials have also struck a more cautious tone.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Easing bank requirements in the current economic environment could have negative countercyclical effects, meaning relief granted at the wrong point in the cycle amplifies rather than dampens the next downturn.
insights.so_what: Timing matters more than direction: capital relief into a late-cycle credit environment raises the amplitude of the next credit drawdown.
insights.quote: easing requirements in the current economic environment could have negative countercyclical effects
insights.locator: Second, can jurisdictional reforms deliver benefits
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Basel Committee Chair Eric Thedeen emphasizes that financial regulation ultimately serves the real economy and that a healthy banking system must be able to absorb shocks while continuing to support businesses and consumers.
insights.so_what: The shock-absorption test is the yardstick the Basel Committee will apply — the standard against which national deviations get judged.
insights.locator: as emphasized by Basel Committee Chair Eric Thedeen
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Basel standards have been adopted by around 70 percent of committee members, but ongoing jurisdictional reviews have led some countries to take a wait-and-see approach, risking further weakening and fragmentation of what are meant to be common standards.
insights.so_what: Regulatory fragmentation raises compliance cost and capital arbitrage opportunity for globally active banks — a structural tailwind for jurisdictional balance-sheet shifting.
insights.locator: Although the Basel standards have been adopted by around 70 percent
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Work underway this year by the Financial Stability Board to assess jurisdictional regulatory modernization and to consult on guiding principles could become the benchmark for the future direction of reform.
insights.so_what: The FSB consultation is the near-term document to read for how much divergence will be tolerated internationally.
insights.locator: Work underway this year by the FSB
insights.speaker: bpiasecki

insights.claim: Rules designed for a different risk and geopolitical environment nearly two decades ago will not always work as originally intended today, so carefully calibrated modernization could capture credit-availability gains without weakening stability safeguards.
insights.so_what: The author's own middle position: the reform is defensible on substance, and the risk is calibration and timing, not direction.
insights.locator: Rules designed for a different risk and geopolitical environment
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
